tldr: By combining automated data generation from geometric primitives like cuboids with two-stage reinforcement learning and distillation, this work achieves a single control policy capable of freely opening and closing articulated tools in-hand across unseen shapes and varied initial grasps.
hero_caption: Overview of ArtManip. Category-level policies are trained in simulation using procedurally generated articulated assets and functional grasps, demonstrating zero-shot transfer to unseen instances, diverse initial grasps, and varied real-world tools.
overview:
When using tools with dexterous hands, humans keep the tool body stable in the palm while deftly operating movable parts like blades or levers with their fingertips. For robots, however, "articulated in-hand manipulation"—actuating an internal joint while maintaining grasp stability on a free-floating base—is extremely difficult. The contact forces applied to move the joint directly act to dislodge the object from the hand, and success heavily depends on how the object was initially held (the initial grasp). Prior studies have been limited to training on single object instances with fixed initial grasps, failing to achieve "category-level generalization" across unseen objects and diverse grasp configurations.

To overcome this, the authors propose an automated generation pipeline based on geometric primitives (such as cuboids) combined with a robust two-stage reinforcement learning framework called "ArtManip." First, the method procedurally generates large quantities of articulated objects in simulation by systematically varying primitive dimensions and joint ranges of motion. Task-oriented functional grasps that can operate the tools are then automatically synthesized using contact-region templates defining allowable fingertip touches. In the policy learning stage, a privileged Teacher policy is trained with randomized joint friction and stiffness alongside a reward curriculum that strengthens grasp stability rewards as learning progresses. This Teacher is distilled into a Student policy relying purely on proprioception (such as joint angle histories), producing a controller that requires no external sensors at deployment.

In experiments using a 22-DoF dexterous hand across four categories—utility knives, lighters, staplers, and tongs—the policy demonstrated strong generalization to unseen instances in simulation. Furthermore, it achieved an 85.7% execution success rate when transferred zero-shot to 12 real-world tools without any additional training. This clearly shows that even a simplified box-primitive simulation environment, if it properly models the essential contact locations and joint dynamics, can successfully transfer to manipulating complex real-world tools.
contributions: Proposed the first category-level articulated in-hand manipulation method capable of generalizing across unseen object instances and diverse initial grasps.
Constructed an automated pipeline combining geometric primitive-based articulated asset generation with functional grasp synthesis using contact-region templates.
Established a robust training strategy integrating articulation physics randomization, a reward curriculum for grasp stability, and closed-loop Teacher-Student distillation.
Demonstrated zero-shot transfer to 12 real-world tools across 4 categories on a physical dexterous hand (22-DoF Sharpa hand), achieving an 85.7% success rate.

sections.heading: Why is manipulating tools inside the hand so difficult?
sections.summary: While rigid-body in-hand manipulation has progressed, manipulating tools with internal joints remains difficult due to tight coupling between base stability and joint actuation. Unlike prior work limited to per-object, per-grasp policies, this work aims for a single category-level policy that generalizes across unseen shapes and varied initial grasps.
sections.details:
When humans use tools such as scissors or lighters, they support the object in the palm to maintain its pose while pushing or pulling movable parts with specific fingers. In recent robotics research, rigid-body in-hand manipulation (such as reposing or rotating cuboids and balls in the palm) has seen tremendous progress.

However, when attempting to manipulate "articulated tools" inside the hand, the difficulty spikes. Unlike objects anchored to the environment such as doors or drawers, a tool held in the hand has a completely free-floating base. Therefore, applying fingertip force to move an internal part generates reaction forces that tend to push the entire tool out of the grasp. In other words, actuating the joint and maintaining a stable grasp on the object are tightly coupled and interfere with each other.

Another major challenge is the high sensitivity to initial grasps. To operate a tool, the fingers must not only prevent drops but also reach the movable component and apply force in the correct direction (a functional grasp). Prior studies on articulated in-hand manipulation were confined to a single specific object with a single human-designed grasp; they could not handle different tool shapes or alternative initial configurations.

Motivated by these challenges, this study proposes "ArtManip," a framework that trains a single policy per category (e.g., all staplers) to reliably open and close tools across unseen geometries and diverse initial grasps.

sections.heading: The intersection of in-hand manipulation and articulated objects: key distinctions from prior work
sections.summary: This section reviews three related areas: dexterous in-hand manipulation, manipulation of anchored articulated objects, and articulated in-hand tool manipulation. This paper is distinct in targeting free-floating articulated objects at the category level without relying on specific instances or fixed grasps.
sections.details:
To clarify where this work stands, consider three lineages of related research:

### 2.1 Dexterous In-hand Manipulation
Reinforcement learning has enabled impressive breakthroughs in reposing and rotating objects using dexterous hands. However, the vast majority of these studies focus on rigid bodies that do not change shape. Actively controlling an object's internal degrees of freedom introduces higher-dimensional contact dynamics, leaving it largely underexplored in in-hand manipulation.

### 2.2 Manipulation of Articulated Objects
Manipulating furniture doors, drawers, and faucets has a long history in robotics. Numerous approaches estimate affordances or joint structures to actuate them using parallel grippers or dexterous hands. However, virtually all of these works assume the object's base is anchored to a table or wall. This differs fundamentally from this paper, where the robot must concurrently support and actuate an unanchored, free-floating base.

### 2.3 In-hand Manipulation of Articulated Objects
Recently, studies have emerged that manipulate tweezers or custom tools in-hand, for example by incorporating contact-adaptive modules. However, these methods were trained specifically on a single object from a single, human-specified initial grasp. As a result, they fail if the tool dimensions change or if the initial grasp shifts slightly. Tackling category-level learning that generalizes to unseen instances and diverse grasps is the decisive distinction of this paper.

sections.heading: Primitive generation and distillation: the technical core of ArtManip
sections.summary: We explain the three-stage pipeline: procedural generation of objects and functional grasps via geometric primitives, privileged Teacher reinforcement learning with randomized joint dynamics, and latent representation distillation into a proprioception-only Student.
sections.details:
The ArtManip pipeline consists broadly of "automated initial configuration construction" and "two-stage reinforcement learning and distillation."

### 3.1 Problem Formulation
The target objects are tools composed of two links connected by a single joint (revolute or prismatic). Given an object instance $m$, an initial functional grasp $\gamma$, and a target joint angle $g$, the goal is to control the hand to drive the joint to the target state without dropping the object.

### 3.2 Initial Configuration Construction
Collecting high-fidelity 3D meshes from scratch is labor-intensive, so the authors procedurally generate tools by assembling geometric primitives like cuboids. By systematically varying link dimensions and joint ranges according to category rules, diverse variations are generated efficiently.
Next comes grasp generation. Existing grasp synthesizers (such as Lightning Grasp) focus solely on preventing drops, often producing grasps where fingers cannot reach the movable part. To resolve this, the authors introduce a single template per category specifying which fingertips may or may not touch each part, synthesizing task-oriented functional grasps under these contact constraints.

### 3.3 Robust Teacher Policy Learning
The privileged Teacher policy is trained using SAPG (Separated Action-Value Policy Gradient). It receives privileged simulation state $\mathbf{o}_t^{\text{priv}}$—such as exact object poses, masses, friction, and joint states—which is compressed into a latent representation $\mathbf{z}_t$ via an MLP encoder before being passed to the policy.
- **Actions**: Commanded joint position deltas, smoothed with a scaling factor $\alpha = 1/40$.
- **Reward Curriculum**: The reward comprises progress toward target $r_{\text{progress}}$, grasp stability $r_{\text{stable}}$, action regularization $r_{\text{regulate}}$, and termination penalty $r_{\text{terminate}}$. Enforcing strong stability from the start causes fingers to freeze, so the weight on $r_{\text{stable}}$ starts small and is gradually increased through a curriculum based on the number of completed opening/closing cycles.
- **Randomization of Joint Dynamics**: Passive joints (knives) receive damping, while spring-loaded joints (tongs, staplers) are modeled with internal PD controllers. Stiffness and damping are randomized across broad ranges to adapt to unknown mechanical resistance.

### 3.4 Latent Representation Learning via Teacher–Student Distillation
Privileged information is unavailable on physical hardware. Therefore, a Student encoder $f_{\text{stu}}$ is trained to predict the Teacher's latent representation $\mathbf{z}$ solely from proprioceptive history (hand joint positions and past actions). Distillation is performed in a closed loop (similar to DAgger), where the environment is rolled out using the Student's predicted latent representation $\mathbf{z}'_t$, preventing distribution shift during physical deployment.

sections.heading: Simulation and real-robot experiments: zero-shot transfer to unseen objects
sections.summary: Evaluations were conducted across four categories: utility knives, lighters, staplers, and tongs. In addition to high generalization and multi-cycle execution on unseen instances in simulation, the policy achieved an 85.7% success rate across 12 real-world tools without fine-tuning.
sections.details:
To validate generalization, comprehensive experiments were performed in simulation and on a real-world 22-DoF Sharpa hand.

### 4.1 Experimental Setup
The target categories comprise utility knives (prismatic joint), lighters, staplers, and tongs (all revolute joints). Each category includes 30 training instances and 5 unseen test instances.
Metrics include Instance Coverage (IC, whether at least one grasp succeeds per object), Grasp Coverage (GC, fraction of successful grasps), Success Rate (SR across all trials), and Consecutive Success Cycles ($\mathrm{CSC}_{\text{mean}}$, $\mathrm{CSC}_{\text{max}}$) measuring repeated opening and closing.
For physical testing, 12 real tools (3 per category) were evaluated. The top 5 promising grasps pre-screened on box-model digital twins were deployed, testing each grasp 5 times (300 trials total).

### 4.2 Results in Simulation
On unseen test instances, the policy achieved 100% IC across all categories. Grasp Coverage (GC) averaged 92.3%, confirming robustness across a wide range of grasp poses rather than relying on a single lucky configuration. Maximum consecutive cycles ($\mathrm{CSC}_{\text{max}}$) averaged 5.6 to 8.6 cycles across categories, demonstrating stable long-horizon manipulation.

### 4.3 Ablation Studies
Scaling the training set for knives from 1 instance (expert baseline) to 5, 10, and 30 instances dramatically increased the unseen-instance SR from 29.4% to 85.0%. Furthermore, when tested on out-of-distribution dimensions (Geo-OOD) and friction/damping (Dyn-OOD), the 30-instance policy maintained high robustness with success rates of 55.5% and 74.9%.

### 4.4 Results in Real World
In zero-shot transfer to 12 physical tools, 257 out of 300 trials succeeded, yielding an 85.7% Success Rate, 88.3% Grasp Coverage, and 100% Instance Coverage. Despite the presence of complex curved surfaces and varied spring stiffness in real tools, the controller trained on simplified box models operated them directly.

sections.heading: Conclusion: simplified models unlock new frontiers in tool manipulation
sections.summary: Combining primitive-based data generation with distillation learning enabled the first category-level in-hand manipulation of articulated tools. It reveals that simplified geometric representations can capture the dynamics essential to the task.
sections.details:
This work tackled the formidable challenge of dexterously operating free-floating articulated tools within a robotic hand.

Key takeaway: even without precise 3D scanned meshes, appropriately arranging geometric primitives and randomizing joint dynamics produces policies that generalize to diverse real-world tools. ArtManip takes a major step toward transforming tool manipulation from a specialized, per-object craft into a generalized skill spanning entire object categories.

sections.heading: Remaining challenges: grasp acquisition and expanded sensing
sections.summary: Three main limitations remain: assuming an initial functional grasp is already established, restricting tools to two links and one joint, and lacking online visual or tactile recovery from slips.
sections.details:
For practical deployment, the authors note the following limitations and directions for future work:

- **Autonomous Grasp Acquisition**: The framework starts from an already established initial functional grasp; it does not model the process of picking up tools from a tabletop into that grasp.
- **Mechanism Complexity**: The study focuses on tools with two links and a single degree of freedom, requiring future extension to complex multi-link mechanisms like scissors or multi-stage linkages.
- **Sensing Modalities**: At deployment, the Student policy relies solely on proprioception (hand joint angles and action histories). Consequently, if fingertips slip significantly or the object shifts during manipulation, it cannot perform closed-loop relocalization using vision or touch.

sections.heading: Appendix: failure mode analysis and training insights
sections.summary: The appendix details physical failure modes (insufficient contact margins and curved-surface slippage), algorithmic comparisons (SAPG vs. PPO), and the necessity of the reward curriculum.
sections.details:
The appendix provides implementation specifics and informative supplementary experimental findings.

### Analysis of Failure Modes
Examining the 7 grasps where all 5 real-world trials failed revealed that fingertip contact was located too close to the boundary of the fingertip pads. When subjected to strong joint reaction forces, the lack of contact margin caused fingers to slide off. This occurred more frequently on utility knives due to high sliding resistance. In addition, local surface curvatures on real tools occasionally caused gradual drift of contact points across repeated cycles (contact migration).

### RL Algorithm and Curriculum Comparisons
Comparing SAPG against standard PPO in Teacher training revealed that PPO suffered from an extended plateau in mid-training, whereas SAPG exhibited steady learning and achieved higher final performance.
Ablation experiments also demonstrated that removing the reward curriculum disrupted the trade-off between stability and joint actuation, severely stalling progress. Omitting the automated functional grasp synthesis pipeline degraded exploration, keeping the learning success rate near 0%, proving each component essential.

takeaways: Simplified assets assembled from geometric primitives like cuboids can achieve zero-shot transfer to diverse real-world tools when articulation physics are appropriately randomized.
Because the search space in articulated in-hand manipulation is vast, constraining exploration beforehand to 'functional grasps' using fingertip contact templates is crucial for success.
Balancing the conflicting objectives of stable base grasping and active joint actuation requires a curriculum that progressively scales up stability rewards.
Distilling the Student policy in a closed loop using its own predicted latent representations (a DAgger-style approach) effectively mitigates distribution shift during real-world deployment.
limitations: Does not cover picking up the tool from a surface to establish the initial functional grasp (Grasp Synthesis / Pick-up), relying on human-placed initial configurations.
Restricted to tools with two links and one degree of freedom; applicability to higher-DoF or multi-link mechanisms remains unverified.
The deployed Student policy relies purely on proprioception, meaning it lacks tactile or visual feedback to recover if fingertips slip unintentionally during manipulation.
